main_damage_causes: Flattening of Aragog's fretful, emotionally erratic personality into a more neutrally menacing figure, losing the specificity of his characterization
Compression of the forest scene removes the detail that Aragog withheld the creature's name even from Hagrid, reducing the layering of his loyalty and limits
Omission of the post-death detail that Aragog's family would have eaten Hagrid without his protection, stripping the most dramatically rich dimension of the Hagrid-Aragog relationship

damaging_scenes.scene: Film CoS Scene 121A – Aragog's hollow encounter
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Aragog as fretful and cautious: he initially orders Harry and Ron killed ('Kill them,' clicked Aragog fretfully), pauses when Hagrid's name is invoked, and engages in extended back-and-forth dialogue. He clicks his pincers furiously when agitated. He is verbally rich, emotionally layered, and his hesitation is a distinct beat that shows Hagrid's hold over him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Aragog is more composed and deliberate, without the 'fretful' quality. The clipped, measured film dialogue omits the fretful clicking agitation ('clicked Aragog fretfully') and the emotional texture of his pauses. His personality is flattened to a functional exposition-delivery role.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's 'fretfully' characterization is a small but specific personality note that distinguishes Aragog from a generic monster. The film renders him more neutrally menacing, losing the nuance that he is old, easily disturbed from sleep, and emotionally erratic rather than coldly calculating.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film CoS Scene 121A – Aragog withholds the name of the creature
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (Scenes 17–20) gives Aragog a full, dramatically weighted refusal: he recalls pleading with Hagrid to let him go when he sensed the beast, makes clear that spiders fear this creature above all others, and explicitly states he never even told Hagrid the creature's name despite being asked many times. This is a multi-beat exchange with urgency and dread.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses this to a single exchange: 'We do not speak of it! It is an ancient creature we spiders fear above all others.' The detail that Aragog never told even Hagrid the name — and was repeatedly asked — is absent. The scene moves immediately to the location clue about the bathroom.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's detail that Aragog withheld the name even from Hagrid deepens both Aragog's characterization (loyal but with limits) and the creature's terror. Its loss is minor but removes a beat that underlines how fearsome the basilisk is and how the spider-Hagrid bond had boundaries.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film CoS Scene 121A – Aragog volunteers the bathroom location
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (Scene 17) has Aragog say: 'The thing that lives in the castle is an ancient creature we spiders fear above all others. Well do I remember how I pleaded with Hagrid to let me go, when I sensed the beast moving about the school.' The bathroom location is then stated: 'The girl was discovered in a bathroom.' In the book, Harry must work to extract even this; Aragog is reluctant and retiring, backing into his web (Scene 21).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Aragog delivers the bathroom line cleanly and without resistance: 'The girl was discovered in a bathroom. When I was accused, Hagrid brought me here.' This is offered almost as parting information before the attack order, making Aragog function as a tidier information-dispensing mechanism.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book Aragog is tiring of talking and physically retreating while his children close in — the information is extracted under mounting terror. The film smooths this into a neater handoff. The damage is limited but Aragog loses some of his indifference to human need.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film CoS Scene 121A – Aragog's farewell line
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book (Scene 23) has Aragog say simply: 'Go? I think not...' — an ominous, minimal line that lets the horror build through the spiders' physical encroachment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Aragog says: 'Go? I think not. My sons and daughters do not harm Hagrid, on my command. But I cannot deny them fresh meat when it wanders so willingly into our midst. Goodbye, friend of Hagrid.' This is a longer, more theatrical speech with a darkly ironic sign-off.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film gives Aragog a more verbose and wryly villainous exit line. 'Goodbye, friend of Hagrid' is a sardonic touch the book does not have. It makes him slightly more self-consciously dramatic and less bleakly indifferent, which is a minor personality shift but not structurally damaging.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film HBP Scene 113 – Aragog's burial: Slughorn asks how Hagrid 'managed to kill it'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (Scenes 64–67) establishes that Hagrid did not kill Aragog — Aragog died of illness, and Hagrid had great difficulty retrieving the body because the other spiders usually eat their dead and had already become hostile to Hagrid after Aragog's death. Hagrid's grief is profound.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Slughorn says: 'My god, dear man. How did you ever manage to kill it?' Hagrid reacts with horror ('Kill 'im! Me oldest friend, 'e was!'). This is a single clumsy line from Slughorn that is quickly corrected by Hagrid's reaction.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Slughorn's mistake is played for a brief awkward beat and immediately corrected by Hagrid. The damage to Aragog's characterization is negligible — the scene recovers quickly and the correction actually reinforces Hagrid's devotion. This is a very minor tonal misstep, not a structural one.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film HBP Scene 113 – Burial scene omits Aragog's family hostility toward Hagrid
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus (Scenes 64–67) establishes a significant and poignant detail: after Aragog's death, his family turned on Hagrid — it was only on Aragog's orders that they never harmed him. Hagrid says: 'Turns out it was only on his orders they didn't eat me!' and notes it was not easy getting the body out. This recontextualizes Aragog's role in their relationship: he was the sole protector of Hagrid among his own kin.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film burial scene (HBP Scene 113) shows Hagrid grieving beside Aragog's body outdoors with no mention of the spider family's hostility or the danger Hagrid faced in retrieving the body. The scene proceeds peacefully with no reference to this dynamic.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This omission removes a key piece of Aragog's characterization: that he was an active protector of Hagrid within a dangerous community, not merely a pet. It also removes dramatic irony — Hagrid's grief is rendered sentimental rather than also being tinged with the revelation that his 'friend' was the only thing standing between him and being eaten. The relationship loses depth.
